paper_title: Gradient Episodic Memory for Continual Learning
mechanism: When computing a gradient update for the current task, GEM checks whether that gradient vector would increase the loss on any previously seen task (stored as a small episodic memory buffer per task). If the inner product between the proposed gradient and any past-task gradient is negative — meaning the update conflicts — GEM projects the proposed gradient to the nearest vector (in L2 sense) that is non-conflicting with all past gradients simultaneously. Non-conflicting updates are applied unchanged. Constraint enforcement is a quadratic program solved per step.
invariant: Gradient direction, not parameter magnitude or recency, determines whether a weight update is harmful. Protecting past performance requires ensuring updates do not point away from past-task optima in gradient space — a condition detectable without replaying full past data, only a small representative memory.
prediction: GEM should exhibit zero or negative backward transfer only when episodic memory is too small to span the relevant gradient subspace of past tasks; with sufficient memory, backward transfer approaches zero and forward transfer remains positive. Ablating the projection (allowing conflicting gradients) should recover catastrophic forgetting.
failure_mode: When episodic memory buffers are too small or unrepresentative (e.g., only one sample per task), the stored gradients poorly approximate the true past-task gradient subspace, the QP constraints become vacuous, and GEM degrades toward fine-tuning with forgetting. Also fails when task boundaries are unavailable at inference, since projection requires knowing which memory belongs to which past task.
source_excerpt: GEM that alleviates forgetting, while allowing beneficial transfer of knowledge to previous tasks. Our experiments on variants of the MNIST and CIFAR-100 datasets demonstrate the strong performance of GEM when compared to the state-of-the-art.

bias_annotation.assumption_note: Minor flags: card accurately notes failure modes but omits QP computational cost scaling and sensitivity to task-boundary assumptions documented in the paper's own limitations.
